title: Review: Solubility equilibria, Ksp, common ion (AP); pH and Kw; Ka, pKa and Kb; pH of weak acids/bases; salt hydrolysis; Neutralization and salts
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AB06#t2 term and clue written for the game; AB04#t3 term and clue written for the game; AB06#t1 term and clue written for the game; AB04#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB04#N.15, AB05#N.12, AB06#N.14, AB05#N.13a, AB06#N.15a, AB02#N.10b, AB04#N.10, AB05#N.5, AB06#N.9, EQ05#N.12, AB02#N.4, AB04#N.4. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Ka
items.clue: Equals [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA] for the equilibrium HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻.

items.label: Parent acid
items.clue: The neutral compound that supplies the anion of a salt, e.g. HNO₃ for KNO₃.

items.label: Hydrolysis
items.clue: The reaction of an ion with water, as when CH₃COO⁻ takes H⁺ and leaves OH⁻.

items.label: Equivalence point
items.clue: The stage on a pH curve where the amounts match the equation, found mid-jump.

questions.stem: Baking powder contains sodium hydrogencarbonate and a solid acid. When the cake batter gets wet, the two react. Why does the cake rise?

options.text: HCO₃⁻ accepts H⁺ from the acid, giving water and carbon dioxide gas.
The acid reacts with sodium, giving hydrogen gas.
A salt and water form, as in every neutralisation, and the steam lifts the cake.
HCO₃⁻ donates H⁺ to the acid, giving CO₃²⁻ and a gas.

questions.explanation: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂. The bubbles of CO₂ make the batter rise, just as CO₂ from a carbonate antacid makes you burp.

questions.stem: Formic acid, HCOOH, has a pKa of 3.75. A formic acid solution is adjusted to pH 3.00 at 25°C. What is the ratio [HCOO⁻]/[HCOOH], and which form predominates?

options.text: 1.0; the two forms are equal in any solution of a weak acid

questions.explanation: [HCOO⁻]/[HCOOH] = Ka/[H₃O⁺] = 10 to the power (pH − pKa) = 10⁻⁰·⁷⁵ = 0.18. The pH is below the pKa, so the acid form predominates.

questions.stem: At 25°C, 50.0 mL of 0.20 M HA(aq), a weak acid with Ka = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶, is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.20 M NaOH(aq). What is the pH of the resulting solution?
questions.explanation: 10 mmol of each react, giving 10 mmol A⁻ in 100.0 mL: [A⁻] = 0.10 M. Kb = Kw/Ka = 2.5 × 10⁻⁹, [OH⁻] = √(2.5 × 10⁻⁹ × 0.10) = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ M, pOH 4.80, pH 9.20.

questions.stem: What is the pH of pure water at this temperature, and is it neutral? At 50 °C, Kw = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴.

options.text: pH 6.63; acidic, as the pH is below 7

questions.explanation: [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so [H⁺] = √(5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.35 × 10⁻⁷ and pH = 6.63. Neutral means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], whatever the pH.

questions.stem: Sodium benzoate, C₆H₅COONa, is a food preservative. Benzoic acid is a weak acid. A solution of sodium benzoate in pure water is alkaline. Which equation explains why?
questions.explanation: Benzoate is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so it takes H⁺ from water and leaves OH⁻. Only a small fraction reacts, so the solution is only mildly alkaline.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.025 M solution of Ba(OH)₂ at 25°C?
questions.explanation: Ba(OH)₂ dissociates completely, giving [OH⁻] = 2 × 0.025 M = 0.050 M. pOH = −log(0.050) = 1.30, and pH = 14.00 − 1.30 = 12.70.

questions.stem: What are the parent acid and parent base of ammonium methanoate, HCOONH₄?

options.text: Parent acid HCOO⁻; parent base NH₄⁺
Parent acid HCOOH; parent base NH₄⁺
Parent acid NH₃; parent base HCOOH
Parent acid HCOOH; parent base NH₃

questions.explanation: The anion HCOO⁻ comes from methanoic acid; the cation NH₄⁺ formed when NH₃ accepted a proton. HCOOH + NH₃ → HCOONH₄.

questions.stem: Benzoic acid has pKa = 4.20. What is its Ka?
questions.explanation: Ka = 10⁻⁴·²⁰ = 6.3 × 10⁻⁵. Sense check: pKa between 4 and 5, so Ka between 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻⁴.

questions.stem: A 0.10 M solution of a weak base, B, is prepared at 25°C. The pKb of B is 4.40. What is the pOH of the solution?
questions.explanation: Kb = 10⁻⁴·⁴⁰ = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵. x² = Kb × 0.10 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶, so x = 2.0 × 10⁻³ M and pOH = 2.70. Only 2% of B ionizes.

questions.stem: Silver chloride has Ksp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C. What is its molar solubility in 0.10 M NaCl(aq) at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.10 M, so Ksp = s × 0.10 and s = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M. That is about 7500 times less than in pure water.

questions.stem: Hydrobromic acid, HBr, is a strong acid. What is the pH of 4.0 × 10⁻³ M HBr(aq)?
questions.explanation: HBr ionises completely, so [H⁺] = 4.0 × 10⁻³ and pH = −log₁₀(4.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.40.

questions.stem: Which reaction produces a salt and water, with no other product?
questions.explanation: Each OH⁻ takes one H⁺ to form water: Ba(OH)₂ + 2HNO₃ → Ba(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O.
